..
Issued at 256 PM EDT Mon Jul 20 2026

Strong thunderstorms marched across the northern portions of the 
U.P. this morning bringing marginally severe hail and isolated 
strong winds gusts. A possible wake low had developed behind the 
thunderstorms bringing strong winds over Lake Superior, particularly 
in the Grand Marais area where gusts reached 60 mph. Visible 
satellite had showed clearing skies over the central and western 
U.P. with the exceptions of a weakening line of showers and 
thunderstorms east of the Keweenaw. This has allowed the western 
part of the U.P. to warm well into the 80s with dewpoints in the 
upper 60s to low 70s, making it feel muggy. Surface pressure 
analysis showed low pressure moving across southern Ontario with the 
associated surface trough extending south into northern MN and the 
central Plains. At the upper levels a well defined shortwave was 
evident over southern Ontario with a strong jet rounding the base of 
the trough. Southwest flow at the surface was helping to advect the 
smoke out of the area with likely continued improvement through the 
day and tonight.

Low pressure over southern Ontario will move east to near James Bay 
by Tuesday morning, dragging a cold front across the U.P. Ahead of 
the front the atmosphere will continue to become more favorable for 
thunderstorms, some of them strong to severe. WOFS shows mlcape 1500-
2500 J/kg along with 45-50kt of deep layer shear. While a cap 
remains in place, with most of the ongoing convection of Lake 
Superior owing to large scale ascent, the cap will weaken through 
the afternoon. Any storms that develop this afternoon could be 
discrete supercells with all thunderstorm hazards on the table. The 
latest WOFS run shows distinct helicity tracks across the central 
U.P. indicative of discrete supercells. There is a non-zero tornado 
threat, especially over the central U.P. where hodographs are deeply 
curved and 0-1 SRH could reach or exceeds 300 m^2/s^2. However, the 
main threats will be large hail (potentially 2" or greater) and 
strong damaging winds (potentially as high as 80mph). As the front 
moves into the area this evening could see the storms build upscale 
into a linear system. If this happens the storms will transition to 
mainly a wind threat has they move east from the central U.P. 
through the eastern U.P. There is still uncertainty as to the 
coverage of thunderstorms. Please continue to monitor the forecast 
and have a way to receive severe weather warnings.

The main hazard is expected this afternoon into the evening as a 
fairly volatile atmosphere for our neck of the woods shapes up. As 
strong synoptic support spreads over the area and airmass recover 
takes place, CAM ensembles suggest MUCAPE values climbing near 2500 
j/kg. What is most impressive is the kinematic environment. Strong 
mid-level flow will increase bulk shear between 45-55 kts and sickle 
shaped low-level hodographs support 0-1 km SRH upwards of 100-200 
m2/s2 (150-250 1-3km SRH). As storm coverage increase ahead of and 
along a surface cold front, all severe weather hazards are on the 
table, including tornadoes should isolated supercells be maintained. 
Steep lapse rates aloft will contribute to a sizable hail threat in 
supercells, potentially 2" or greater. Once storms grow upscale into 
a more linear segment, damaging winds will then become the main 
threat. SPC has maintained a Slight Risk (level 2 of 5) for the 
entire UP with an area of the west and central UP in an Enhanced 
Risk (level 3 of 5) for severe weather. All of this is to say that 
if you have outdoor plans today, especially in the afternoon and 
evening, have a way to receive a warning and a plan should one be 
issued.

Expect cooler conditions on Tuesday into Wednesday behind the cold 
front that will sweep through the area tonight. High temperatures 
will be mainly in the 70s with 60s possible close to Lake Superior. 
It will be breezy on Tuesday with north winds potentially gusting to 
30 mph over the land areas and over 45 mph over the Great Lakes. 
Some lingering showers are likely for the NW wind "snowbelts" and 
upslope favored areas on Tuesday as 850 mb temps cool between 5-10C. 
This may aid in lake-enhanced showers as the nearshores and areas of 
the west and central lake have warmed between 15-20C. Swim 
conditions will become dangerous on Tuesday for the Lake Superior 
beaches of Marquette and Alger County. 

The area remains under northwest flow aloft into the early part of 
the weekend with a ridge building back over the central U.S. This 
will bring the opportunity for showers and thunderstorms as weak 
disturbances in the flow push across the U.P. Afternoon temperatures 
will be seasonable, upper 70s to low 80s, with lows in the 50s. 
Temperatures will warm to the mid 80s on Sunday as the ridge shifts 
east over the Upper Great Lakes.
